Twelve months on, that cost line is unchanged: applications have risen by about a third and the same team has absorbed the increase without additional staff. The service head regards this as a clear success, while the finance business partner records the benefit as unrealised. Both are describing the same facts. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Record what has actually occurred as a capacity benefit against a stated measure, kept separate from the cash saving that was approved.
options.rationale: Absorbing a third more work without extra staff is a real gain and deserves a stated measure rather than an argument. Keeping it separate from the approved saving stops one being quietly substituted for the other.

options.text: Put the difference between the approved cash benefit and the realised capacity benefit to the sponsor as a decision about the case.
options.rationale: The council funded a reduction in processing cost and has received something else, which is a change to the basis of the investment. Only the sponsor can decide whether that substitution is acceptable.

options.text: Report the benefit as realised, since the processing cost for each application has fallen exactly as forecast.
options.rationale: It reports the mechanism as though it were the outcome. Cost per application was how the saving was to be produced; the saving itself was what was approved, and it has not appeared.

options.text: Ask the service to reduce the team to the size the original case assumed and take the saving.
options.rationale: It subordinates a live operational judgement to a year-old projection. The extra applications may well be worth more than the saving, and that is the service's call rather than the project's.

options.text: Write off the cash benefit and close the case as delivered.
options.rationale: It closes the question instead of answering it, and discards the most useful lesson available: that the forecast rested on an assumption about redeployment nobody had ever agreed with the service.

questions.explanation: A benefit is realised only in the form it was approved in, so a genuine gain of a different kind is still a change to the case and belongs in front of whoever funded it. Cases that convert saved effort into money almost always carry an unstated assumption that the effort will be removed rather than reused, and that assumption is the one worth surfacing early. Both parties here can be right at once, which is exactly why the decision is not the project manager's to settle.
questions.mindset: A different benefit from the one you promised is still a change to the case.

questions.stem: A programme assurance reviewer at a transport authority has listed three observations from a delivery programme and proposed the same remedy for all of them, which is tighter estimation discipline. You think each observation points at a different problem, and that none of them is about effort. Match each symptom to what it most likely indicates about value. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Every feature the team ships is accepted by the sponsor, and none of them moves any measure named in the business case.
Stakeholders keep requesting features that already exist in the released product.
The benefit forecast has not been revised in two years, across three changes of sponsor.

options.text: The link between what is being built and the outcomes it was meant to move has never been drawn.
options.rationale: Acceptance confirms a deliverable meets its criteria, which is a statement about the thing rather than about its effect. Features can pass every check and still connect to nothing in the case.

options.text: Delivered capability is not reaching the people it was built for.
options.rationale: A request for something that already exists is evidence that it was never found or never explained. The build was complete and the delivery, in the sense that matters, was not.

options.text: The case has stopped being a live document and become a historical record.
options.rationale: Two years and three sponsors is more than enough change to have moved something in the forecast. A number that never moves is one nobody is using to make decisions.

options.text: The team's effort estimates are unreliable.
options.rationale: Not used. Estimation accuracy is about predicting how long work takes, and none of these three symptoms concerns effort at all. Reaching for it is how a value problem gets diagnosed as a delivery problem.

questions.explanation: Value problems present through delivery symptoms and are routinely misread as delivery problems, because delivery is what everyone is watching. Sorting them means asking whether the failure lies in the link from output to outcome, in the capability reaching its users, or in the case having gone stale. Each of those has a different remedy, and applying the wrong one leaves the symptom intact and everyone busier.
questions.mindset: Diagnose the symptom before reaching for the remedy you know best.

questions.stem: An agile programme is building a patient-triage tool. The product owner considers it releasable once clinicians can complete a triage. The sponsor wants the reporting pack finished before any release, because that is what the board sees. The regulator's inspector will not accept a live clinical tool without a full audit trail. Each position is reasonable, and none has shifted in six weeks. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Get the three positions written into one release-readiness definition, with the regulator's requirement set as a constraint and the other two ranked within it.
options.rationale: It separates a condition that cannot be waived from two that are preferences, which is the distinction the stalemate has been missing. Once the floor is fixed, the remaining disagreement is an ordinary ranking question the team can settle.

options.text: Release on the product owner's definition, since the product owner owns the backlog and its priorities.
options.rationale: It applies backlog authority to a decision that contains a regulatory condition no product owner can waive. Ownership of ranking is not ownership of what makes a release lawful.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor for a ruling, since he controls the budget.
options.rationale: It settles a disagreement by rank when one of the three positions is not the sponsor's to overrule. Any ruling that waives the audit trail collapses on first contact with the inspector.

options.text: Build all three and release once every requirement is complete in full.
options.rationale: It avoids the trade-off by satisfying everybody, which is the most expensive route available and defers clinical benefit for as long as the longest item takes.

questions.explanation: A stalemate between reasonable positions is usually a sign that constraints and preferences have not been separated. Conditions imposed from outside set a floor beneath which no release can go, and everything above that floor is ranking, which is a solvable problem. Working the two together produces either an unlawful release or an unaffordable one, and six weeks of unchanged positions is the signal that nobody has done the sorting.
questions.mindset: Separate the conditions that cannot be waived from the ones that can, then rank only the second kind.

questions.stem: A finance partner at a regional water company is reviewing how two of your projects will be judged. One reports progress as a percentage of planned deliverables completed; the other has forecast a saving that will land in an accounts line several unrelated initiatives also touch. She wants to know what each arrangement can and cannot establish. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The dashboard figure showing 84 per cent of planned deliverables complete cannot establish
A saving visible only in an accounts line that many other things also affect calls for

options.text: whether any of the value the programme was funded for has yet appeared
options.rationale: Completion counts output against plan, and a plan can be executed immaculately while the outcome it was built for does not move. It is a measure of conformance, not of worth.

options.text: an agreed method for isolating the project's contribution, fixed before the change goes live
options.rationale: Where several influences land on one line, attribution has to be settled in advance or it becomes an argument afterwards between people with different interests. Fixing the method early is what makes the eventual figure credible.

options.text: a monthly report circulated to everyone with an interest in the project
options.rationale: Not used. Circulating a figure more widely does nothing to establish whose figure it is. It answers a communication question when the difficulty in both sentences is measurement, which is the standard way a measurement problem gets treated as a reporting one.

questions.explanation: A measure answers the question it was built to answer and no other, so the discipline is to check what a number was designed for before relying on it for something else. Deliverable completion reports conformance to a plan; benefit realisation reports worth; and where a benefit lands in a shared line, the method of attribution has to be agreed before the change rather than negotiated once the figures are in and everyone has a position to defend.
questions.mindset: Ask what question a measure was built to answer before you rely on it for another.
